definition: The nyiso-238 keeper's recipe, UNCHANGED, on a REPAIRED C1 BENCHMARK. Zero ScenarioConfig fields move: this bundle is 2026-09-16-nyiso-238-hydro-budget replayed byte-faithfully (replay_keeper.py, no --set, four per-year shards at pinned SHA 3edb8ad8), verified against that keeper's committed class hourlies at a worst per-class deviation of 5.0e-7 TWh over four years. The MODEL therefore still carries exactly one field versus its own predecessor -- hydro_budget_period_by_instrument True, the Niagara 24 h / St Lawrence 168 h published instrument periods, zero free parameters. WHAT MOVED IS THE BENCHMARK. reconcile_vintage_classes scaled the EIA-923 grid-delivered fossil classes to EIA-930's gas+coal cell ALONE. EIA-923 books a plant's MWh under the fuel it BURNED, so a dual-fuel unit's oil hours land in the 923 `oil` class while its gas hours stay in the CC/CT/ST classes; EIA-930 books the same generation under NG: OIL. The comparison straddled a fuel boundary and read an ATTRIBUTION difference as a LEVEL error -- the identical failure the function already refuses to propagate one fuel over. Oil now joins the family on BOTH sides. NYISO 2022 read +5.13 % gas-only (fired, deflating every fossil class by x0.951167) and reads +0.08 % with oil on both sides (does not fire), the tightest agreement of any complete NYISO vintage. DETERMINATION: CALIBRATED (grade 7 of 8, fails 0, C3c the lone ledgered caveat), from NOT-YET. Every C1 row passes in every gated year; C1-2022 CC_REGULAR goes +4.81 TWh / +3.62 pp FAIL -> +3.14 TWh / +2.95 pp PASS. Zero PASS -> FAIL flips. STATED AT FULL MAGNITUDE: that share leg passes by ~0.05 pp of a +/-3.0 pp band, and the model's +3.14 TWh CC_REGULAR 2022 over-run is REAL and remains this lane's open object -- NYC is 88 % of the plant-level miss and February plus November are 61 % of the annual miss. The repair corrects how that miss is MEASURED, not the miss. The G2 hydro energy loss (-55.2 / -25.5 GWh in 2022 / 2023) carries over as a LEDGERED OPEN ROOT-CAUSE ISSUE, not an accepted limitation.
market_story: TWO METERS, ONE FLEET. New York's downstate combined cycles and steam units are dual-fuel: they burn gas until the winter basis makes oil cheaper or the pipeline is curtailed, then they burn oil, and the same physical machine keeps serving the same load. The two federal surveys record that fleet differently. EIA-923 is a monthly plant survey filed by FUEL, so a dual-fuel plant's gas-fired MWh stay with its combined-cycle class and only its liquid burn is booked as `oil`. EIA-930 is hourly BA telemetry, and through 2022 and the first half of 2023 NYISO's feed carried a flat ~550 MW block under Petroleum every single month -- a classification, not a burn: New York's liquid fleet is peaking plant that runs in cold snaps, not a baseload. NYISO's own published fuel mix settles it, because the ISO does not publish an oil category at all: an oil-capable unit is filed under `Dual Fuel`, and the ISO's fossil total for 2022 is 65.7 TWh against EIA-930's gas cell of 60.3. WHY IT REACHED THE MODEL'S SCORE. The benchmark reconciles the EIA-923 class actuals to EIA-930's grid total, because that is the delivered basis the model is scored on. Comparing 923's gas classes against 930's gas cell alone made 2022 look like EIA-923 had over-stated New York's fossil generation by 5 %, and the reconcile duly marked every fossil class down by 4.9 % -- 1.6 TWh of it on CC_REGULAR. The model had not changed; the ruler had. WHAT THE MODEL STILL GETS WRONG. Measured against the corrected actual, New York's combined cycles still run 3.1 TWh hot in 2022, and the miss is concentrated where a market story would put it: 88 % in New York City, and 61 % of it in February and November -- the shoulder-cold months when the real fleet switched to oil, ran on price rather than on gas economics, or sat behind a pipeline constraint the model does not represent. In July through September, when the constraint is heat rather than fuel delivery, the model runs those same units COLD. That asymmetry is the next object, and it is a fuel-and-deliverability question, not a benchmark one.
